prompt: A user replaced their laptop's display assembly at a repair shop. Since then, Wi-Fi signal is very weak even next to the access point, but a USB Wi-Fi adapter works fine.

options.text: Switch the router to 2.4 GHz only, because the lower band penetrates walls better and so improves a weak signal
Replace the wireless card with a new one, since weak reception next to the access point means the card has failed
Update the wireless driver to the latest version from the manufacturer, in case the repair left an older driver loaded
Check that the Wi-Fi antenna leads in the display lid were reconnected to the card

explanation: Laptop Wi-Fi antennas run through the display lid, so a screen replacement is the classic moment for a lead to be left unplugged or pinched. The timing points to the repair, not the card or driver. A USB adapter working proves the network itself is fine.

prompt: A company lets staff read work email on personal phones. When someone leaves, IT must remove company data without touching personal photos.

options.text: MDM with a work profile or container and a selective wipe that removes only company data
A full remote wipe through MDM, which removes company data quickly but also erases the employee's personal photos
Ask the employee to delete the mail app and sign out of the work account
Disable the user's cellular data in the carrier portal, which blocks mail sync but leaves the company data on the phone

explanation: BYOD management separates business apps and data into a managed container or work profile. A selective wipe removes only that container. A full wipe would destroy personal data on a device the company does not own, and asking the user relies on trust rather than control.

prompt: A user wants to read the same mailbox on a phone, a laptop, and a tablet, with read status and folders staying in sync.

options.text: POP3 on port 110, which downloads mail to one client and usually removes it from the server
IMAP on port 143 (or IMAPS on 993), which keeps mail on the server and syncs state to every device
SMTP on port 25, which relays outgoing mail between servers, not a synced mailbox view
LDAP on port 389, which looks up directory entries such as contacts but does not store or synchronize mail messages

explanation: IMAP keeps mail on the server and syncs state to every client. POP3 downloads messages and usually removes them from the server, so other devices miss them. SMTP sends mail between servers, and LDAP queries directories.

prompt: Several PCs on one floor suddenly cannot browse the web. ipconfig shows addresses in the 169.254.0.0/16 range and no default gateway.

options.text: The NIC drivers are corrupt on every PC
The proxy settings are wrong
The PCs cannot reach a DHCP server
The DNS server is down

explanation: A 169.254.x.x address is APIPA, which Windows assigns itself when no DHCP server answers. Because it affects a whole floor, check the DHCP server, its scope, or the switch and VLAN serving that floor. A DNS failure would leave a valid IP address in place.

prompt: A new access point must be mounted on a warehouse ceiling 60 m from the network closet. There is no power outlet at the mounting point, and the cable will run through an air-handling space.

options.text: Plenum-rated Cat 6 with PoE from the switch or an injector, rated for air-handling spaces
Direct burial Cat 6a with a power injector, which suits underground runs but is not rated for air-handling spaces
Multimode fiber with a local power adapter, but the ceiling has no outlet
Cat 5 UTP with an extension cord run along the cable, which supplies power but ignores fire code and the speed the access point needs

explanation: Air-handling spaces require plenum-rated cable for fire safety, 60 m is within copper's 100 m limit, and PoE delivers power over the same cable. Fiber carries no power, and direct burial cable is for underground runs, not plenum spaces.

prompt: A small office wants a NAS with four drives. It must keep working if any two drives fail at the same time.

options.text: RAID 0 across four drives, which stripes data for speed and capacity but loses everything when any one drive fails
RAID 6, which uses double parity across the four drives
RAID 1 with four drives in mirrored pairs, which survives some failures but loses data if the two drives of one pair fail
RAID 5 with four drives, which stripes data with single parity and so survives one drive failure but not two

explanation: RAID 6 uses double parity and survives any two drive failures, with at least four drives. RAID 5 survives only one. RAID 0 has no redundancy at all. RAID 10 would also use four drives, but it survives two failures only if they are in different mirror pairs, not any two.

prompt: A technician tries to create a 64-bit virtual machine in a Type 2 hypervisor on a new desktop. The hypervisor reports that hardware virtualization is unavailable.

options.text: Install more RAM, because the hypervisor needs memory for a 64-bit guest and reports unavailable hardware when it is short on the host
Enable Intel VT-x or AMD-V in the UEFI settings, since hardware virtualization is often switched off by default in firmware
Switch to a Type 1 hypervisor, which runs directly on the hardware and so does not need CPU virtualization features, at the cost of reinstalling the host
Convert the disk from MBR to GPT, since 64-bit guests need GPT partitioning on the host to be created

explanation: Hardware virtualization support is often disabled by default in firmware. Enabling it in UEFI is the fix. Changing the hypervisor type does not help, because both types need the CPU feature, and neither RAM nor the partition style affects this error.

prompt: A startup wants to deploy its web application without managing operating systems, patches, or runtime versions. It only wants to upload code.

options.text: PaaS, where the platform runs the OS and runtime and the customer uploads only code
IaaS
Private cloud
SaaS

explanation: PaaS provides the OS and runtime, and the customer supplies the application and data. IaaS would leave the team patching VMs. SaaS is a finished application that the customer uses, not a platform for their own code. Private cloud is a deployment model, not a service model.

prompt: An office desktop loses the correct date and time whenever it is unplugged overnight. Several websites then show certificate warnings.

options.text: Reinstall Windows to rebuild the system clock service, since the OS is keeping the time wrongly after each shutdown
Replace the power supply, because a weak supply fails to keep the clock powered while the computer is unplugged
Replace the network card, since time synchronization through NTP fails and so the clock drifts after each restart
Replace the CMOS battery

explanation: The coin-cell CMOS battery keeps the real-time clock running without mains power. When it dies, the clock resets. A clock far in the past or future makes valid certificates appear expired or not yet valid, which explains the browser warnings.

prompt: Pages from a laser printer show toner that smears and rubs off when touched.

options.text: Low toner, which would show as faded or streaked prints, not toner that rubs off
A wrong printer driver, which usually produces garbled text, not smeared toner
A worn pickup roller, which causes misfeeds and jams but does not affect toner adhesion
A failing fuser assembly, which no longer bonds the toner to the paper using heat and pressure

explanation: The fuser uses heat and pressure to bond toner to the paper. If it fails, toner sits loose on the page and smears. Low toner causes faded prints, a wrong driver causes garbled output, and worn pickup rollers cause feeding problems.
